speaker: Doctor
text: I see you're having trouble walking, controlling your bladder, and speaking clearly. Have you noticed any weakness or numbness in your legs or arms?

speaker: Patient
text: 54-year-old male. The patient has been experiencing a gradual difficulty in walking over the past 3 months, requiring wheelchair assistance for the last month. Additionally, there is a history of urinary incontinence for 1 year and recent onset of speech slurring making communication challenging.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for those details. To better localize the issue, have you noticed any changes in your sense of touch or temperature sensation in your legs? Additionally, have you experienced any involuntary muscle spasms or tremors?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Progressive difficulty walking. I also have Urinary incontinence, Slurred speech, Rigidity in limbs, Mild hand tremor, Orthostatic hypotension.

speaker: Doctor
text:
The combination of gait difficulties, urinary incontinence, speech slurring, and limb rigidity strongly suggests a neurological disorder affecting the brainstem and cerebellum. Given your age and the progression of symptoms over months, could you tell me if you have experienced any falls or recent head trauma? Also, do you have any history of high blood pressure or smoking?

REQUEST TEST: MRI Brain with contrast; REQUEST TEST: Urinalysis.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: MRI Brain with contrast: Multiple areas of atrophy and signal changes in the brainstem, cerebellum, and basal ganglia, consistent with neurodegenerative processes. Urinalysis: Appearance Clear, WBC 0-5 /HPF, RBC 0-2 /HPF, Nitrites Negative, Leukocyte Esterase Negative.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Multiple System Atrophy (MSA). The combination of cerebellar ataxia (gait difficulty, slurred speech), autonomic dysfunction (orthostatic hypotension, urinary incontinence), and parkinsonism (rigidity, tremor), along with MRI findings of brainstem and cerebellar atrophy, is highly suggestive of MSA-C or MSA-P. Given the prominent cerebellar signs, MSA-C is more likely.
